settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: load-external-dtd=false is explicitly set, which in many (Xerces-based) configurations blocks external DTD fetching.
XmlUtils.getTextForElement returns null on parse exception and only extracts simple element text, which limits some payload classes; parse failures are logged, not fatal.
candidates.description: XmlUtils.getXmlReader() builds an XMLReader via SAXParserFactory.newInstance() and sets only three features: namespaces=true, namespace-prefixes=false, and nonvalidating/load-external-dtd=false. It does not disable external-general-entities, external-parameter-entities or XInclude. getTextForElement()/getTextForElements() then parse arbitrary XML strings supplied by callers (SAML/CAS responses and SLO logout messages). Depending on the underlying SAX implementation, external entities or parameter entities defined in the internal subset may still be resolvable, giving a file-read/SSRF/entity-expansion surface. The same pattern appears in Cas20ServiceTicketValidator.extractCustomAttributes(), which calls SAXParserFactory.newInstance() then setNamespaceAware(true)/setValidating(false) and parses the server response with no entity-related hardening.
missing_evidence: The actual SAX parser implementation/runtime dependency (JDK built-in vs Xerces) and its default for external-general-entities on the target platform was not read.
No test or configuration file was read that demonstrates whether external entity expansion actually succeeds.
preconditions: Attacker can influence the XML string parsed by XmlUtils.getTextForElement/getTextForElements or Cas20ServiceTicketValidator.extractCustomAttributes (e.g. CAS/SAML server response content, or an unauthenticated SLO 'logoutRequest' payload).
Deployed XML parser resolves external entities even when nonvalidating/load-external-dtd is false.
candidates.title: XML parsing helpers disable external DTD but not external entity expansion / XInclude

counter_evidence: The mapping is typically keyed on the CAS service ticket which the attacker normally does not know for victim sessions, so blind guessing is hard.
isMultipartRequest() blocks multipart-encoded bodies, and destroySession only acts when a mapping exists for the token.
safeParameters restricts which parameters are read from POST requests when the ticket parameter is configured to be URL-only.
candidates.description: SingleSignOutHandler treats a POST request carrying the logoutParameterName ('logoutRequest') as a logout command if it is not multipart, extracts 'SessionIndex' text from the (attacker-supplied) XML body via XmlUtils.getTextForElement, then looks up and invalidates the session mapped to that token. Separately, recordSession() maps an arbitrary, unauthenticated 'ticket' request parameter to the current HttpSession. There is no verification in the reviewed code that the logout message originates from the trusted CAS server (no signature/allow-list/source check), and the mapping is keyed on a client-supplied value. An attacker who can reach the endpoint can therefore attempt to force session invalidation (logout/DoS) for tokens it can guess or for sessions whose token it can cause to be registered. process() returns false to stop the chain and the request body is read only through CommonUtils.safeGetParameter, which does not add authentication.
missing_evidence: No network/source filtering, shared-secret validation, or CAS server certificate check was read in SingleSignOutHandler or SingleSignOutFilter.
The SessionMappingStorage implementations (HashMap-backed, etc.) were not read in this session, so lookup semantics/expiry are unverified.
Integration deployments (Tomcat valves) that may add transport-level restrictions were not read.
preconditions: SingleSignOutFilter (or an integration valve) is deployed and mapped to a reachable URL.
Attacker can send unauthenticated POST requests with the configured logout parameter name.
Attacker knows or can guess/induce a SessionIndex token that exists in the session mapping storage.
candidates.title: Back-channel SLO destroys sessions based on unauthenticated logoutRequest and unauthenticated ticket mapping

counter_evidence: The SAML artifact is normally validated by the CAS server against its own ticket registry, so injected elements would still have to satisfy server-side ticket validation.
No evidence was read that the CAS server parses the SOAP envelope in a way that makes the injected content security-relevant.
candidates.description: Saml11TicketValidator.retrieveResponseFromServer() builds a SOAP SAML Request by string concatenation and inserts the caller-supplied ticket directly inside <samlp:AssertionArtifact>%s</samlp:AssertionArtifact> with no XML escaping or validation. The ticket value flows from AbstractTicketValidationFilter.doFilter -> retrieveTicketFromRequest(request) (an attacker-controlled request parameter) into validate(ticket, service) and then into this method. Content-Length is computed from the unescaped string length and the body is written verbatim, so a ticket containing XML metacharacters can alter the SOAP/SAML envelope sent to the CAS server (SOAP/SAML parameter or element injection), potentially influencing validation semantics at the server.
missing_evidence: retrieveTicketFromRequest() (in AbstractTicketValidationFilter, lines ~1-120 were read as context only peripherally) and any ticket-format validation were not confirmed to be absent.
No server-side parsing behaviour or test was read to demonstrate impact.
preconditions: A SAML 1.1 validation filter/validator is configured and reachable.
Attacker can supply a crafted 'ticket' request parameter whose value is passed unchanged to the validator.
candidates.title: Ticket value concatenated into SAML SOAP request without XML escaping

counter_evidence: The service value IS URL-encoded via encodeUrl() before being added, so the most clearly attacker-controlled parameter is protected.
customParameters are deployment configuration, not directly attacker-supplied in the normal flow.
candidates.description: AbstractUrlBasedTicketValidator.constructValidationUrl() builds the CAS validation URL by concatenating the casServerUrlPrefix, suffix and then each urlParameters entry as key + '=' + value without encoding the key or the already-encoded value. The 'ticket' value is inserted directly (only 'service' goes through encodeUrl). Custom parameters (setCustomParameters) are merged afterwards and likewise appended raw, and in the Saml11 subclass populateUrlAttributeMap moves the encoded 'service' into a TARGET parameter. If any of these values (ticket, custom parameters) are attacker-influenced, additional query parameters can be injected into the validation request, potentially altering what the CAS server is asked to validate/authorize.
missing_evidence: Whether ticket content is validated elsewhere (e.g. by retrieveTicketFromRequest or the filter) before reaching this method was not fully read.
No test demonstrating parameter injection through the ticket value was read.
preconditions: Attacker can influence the ticket value or a configured custom parameter that is placed into the validation URL.
The 'ticket' value is not otherwise validated/constrained before reaching constructValidationUrl.
candidates.title: Validation URL assembled by raw string concatenation of unencoded parameter values

counter_evidence: When 'service' is configured explicitly it takes precedence and the header-based logic is skipped (constructServiceUrl lines 272-274).

The final redirect target is built appending request.getRequestURI(), so full external-host control depends on header/casing behaviour; matching requires the configured name to contain the header value.
candidates.description: CommonUtils.findMatchingServerName() selects the configured server name by comparing request.getHeader("Host") and request.getHeader("X-Forwarded-Host") against configured server names, and constructServiceUrl() then builds the service URL from the matched server plus request.getRequestURI() and the raw query string. Host and X-Forwarded-Host are client-controllable headers; when the configured serverNames contain a value that sub-string-matches the attacker's Host, an attacker-chosen host component can be reflected into the service URL that is sent to the CAS server and used in post-validation redirects (response.sendRedirect(constructServiceUrl(...)) in AbstractTicketValidationFilter). Additionally, the comparison uses lowerCaseServer.contains(comparisonHost) and only lower-cases the configured server (not the header), which is a loose match.
missing_evidence: No proxy/servlet-container configuration was read that would normalize or reject Host/X-Forwarded-Host.
No test exercising an attacker-controlled Host header against multi-value serverNames was read.
preconditions: The filter is configured with a space-separated list of serverNames (multiple entries) rather than a fixed 'service' URL.
The attacker can control the Host/X-Forwarded-Host header reaching the application (e.g. no fronting proxy that rewrites it).
candidates.title: Service URL construction trusts client-supplied Host / X-Forwarded-Host headers

counter_evidence: The result length returned comes from decompresser.inflate(result), so the code uses only the bytes actually produced and does not over-read.
Inflate is bounded by the pre-allocated buffer, so it cannot expand beyond 10x in memory; the primary impact would be truncation/DoS rather than memory disclosure.
isFrontChannelLogoutRequest requires GET and a non-blank parameter only; no additional amplification factor is proven.
candidates.description: SingleSignOutHandler.uncompressLogoutMessage() base64-decodes the attacker-supplied frontLogoutParameterName value and inflates it into a fixed-size buffer of binaryMessage.length * 10 (DECOMPRESSION_FACTOR). It neither bounds the plaintext size nor checks whether inflation completed (decompresser.finished()), and it does not limit the size of the incoming baseline64 message. A highly compressible payload that inflates beyond 10x the compressed length will be silently truncated, and an attacker can force repeated decompression of large inputs, giving a resource-consumption / message-corruption surface on the front-channel SLO path.
missing_evidence: Real-world impact (CPU/memory amplification magnitude) was not measured; no profiling or test of large payloads was read.
Whether any upstream container limit constrains request parameter size was not read.
preconditions: Front-channel SLO (SingleSignOutFilter) is deployed and reachable via GET with the configured front logout parameter.
Attacker can send arbitrary large base64-deflate data.
candidates.title: Front-channel logout decompression uses fixed 10x output buffer with no size bound
